records.name_note: Lead name is Herbst's bloodleaf, the rendered subtitle under the H1 of the RHS dedicated page for Iresine herbstii; Bloodleaf and Joseph's Coat are already used in this catalog for other species, and Beefsteak sits too close to the catalog's existing Beefsteak Plant (Perilla). NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is, alphabetized, Beefsteak, Bloodleaf, Chicken Gizzard, Chicken-Gizzard, Formosa Bloodleaf, Joseph's Coat, Yellow Bloodleaf; RHS lists beef plant, beefsteak plant, chicken gizzard under Other common names. The accepted name splits between sources: NC State's H1 is Iresine diffusa f. herbstii with Iresine herbstii under Previously known as, while the RHS dedicated page is headed Iresine herbstii and marks that name as correct. The bare binomial Iresine herbstii (the given name) is recorded as accepted.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for this plant has no Poison block; the only toxicity evidence is its tags, which include #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for dogs and #non-toxic for horses. The full tag set on that page is: #red leaves #purple leaves #showy leaves #interiorscape #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #container plant #perennial #annual #variegated #low growing #border. The RHS page carries no toxicity statement.
unknowns: MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org kempercode b603) could not be loaded from the sandbox, so no MoBot evidence was used; UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD and UGA were not found to have a dedicated page for this taxon.
Accepted name conflict: NC State files it as Iresine diffusa f. herbstii (previously Iresine herbstii); RHS lists Iresine herbstii with Name Status Correct. Recorded the bare binomial.

Size conflict: NC State Dimensions (Height 1 ft 0 in - 1 ft 6 in, Width 1 ft 0 in - 3 ft 0 in) used as the anchor (12-18 in tall, 12-36 in wide). RHS gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), and NC State prose says it can grow 5 feet tall and 3 feet wide in its native habitat.
soil_base left null: no admissible species-specific potting-mix statement; RHS's Under glass compost sentence is genus-level boilerplate for Iresine and was not used.
fertilize_* left null: the only fertiliser advice found is RHS's genus-level Under glass paragraph, which was not used as species evidence.
soil_ph left null: RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral (no bounds); NC State has no pH field.
water_regime keep_moist is read from NC State's houseplant watering sentence; no dry-down depth or day interval is stated.
NC State carries no Attracts field and RHS no pollinator tag, so attracts_pollinators is null; neither source addresses edibility, so is_edible is null.
direct_sun_hours_max null: NC State's 6-or-more-hours figure is the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose.
No source states a chill-damage onset temperature, day/night temperatures, humidity or light in foot-candles; all left null.
RHS's H1C hardiness rating and NC State's USDA zones 10a-12b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Ipomoea lobata page renders a Common Name(s) list of Firecracker Vine, Fire Vine, Spanish Flag (alphabetical if spaces are ignored; same order as its <title> parenthetical), and its Description calls the plant Spanish flag. RHS's dedicated page renders 'Spanish flag' under its H1 (page title 'Ipomoea lobata | Spanish flag'), and MoBot's dedicated page (taxonid=279323; it reads in a browser but refuses non-browser fetchers) gives Common Name Spanish flag and says 'commonly called Spanish flag vine or firecracker vine'. So two of three dedicated pages lead with Spanish flag. Firecracker Vine was kept because it is the first item of NC State's Common Name(s) list. Former names: Mina lobata and Quamoclit lobata (NC State 'Previously known as'). RHS's Synonyms field lists Ipomoea lobata 'Exotic Love', Ipomoea versicolor and Mina lobata, RHS has a separate Mina lobata page whose Name Status is Synonym, and MoBot says 'Synonymous with Mina lobata.'
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Ipomoea lobata page), Poison block, which is human-scoped ("Poisonous to Humans"): Poison Severity: Low (the page also states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms: Vomiting, large amounts of seeds may cause hallucinations. Poison Toxic Principle: Indole alkaloids (Lysergic acid, lysergamide, elymoclavine and chanoclavine). Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Seeds. Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State's Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, and its tag line reads "#problem for horses #problem for dogs #problem for cats #vine #herbaceous perennial #annual #frost tender #colorful #long bloom season"; the page gives no cat/dog-specific symptoms or severity. Plant Type per NC State: Annual, Herbaceous Perennial, Vine. RHS (dedicated Ipomoea lobata page) is broader and not part-restricted: its Potentially harmful field reads "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and its Pets line reads "Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants", which names no animal, so it is not used for toxic_to_pets. The sources differ in scope: NC State limits the poison part to seeds and rates severity low, while RHS states harmful if eaten without naming a part.
unknowns: MoBot's dedicated page (https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=279323) refuses this environment's non-browser fetchers (ConnectError), so verify_quotes cannot check it, but it reads in a browser (read by the auditor). Its structured fields give Common Name Spanish flag, Zone 10 to 11, Height 10.00 to 16.00 feet, Spread 1.00 to 2.00 feet, Sun Full sun, Water Medium, and Attracts Hummingbirds, Butterflies. Its Culture says 'Best grown in evenly moist, rich, well-draining soil in full sun.' and 'Tolerant of some shade, but will not produce as showy of a floral display.' Its Noteworthy Characteristics say 'Ipomoea lobata, commonly called Spanish flag vine or firecracker vine, ...' and 'Synonymous with Mina lobata.' It gives no toxicity, pH or edibility. No field value was taken from it. Clemson HGIC returned 403, and no admissible UF/IFAS page for this species was found.

is_edible is false only on RHS's unscoped 'Harmful if eaten'; NC State rates poison severity Low and names Seeds as the poison part, so the two sources differ in scope. No admissible source says any part is grown or used for food.
toxic_to_pets is true only from NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags; the page gives no cat/dog symptoms or severity. RHS's Pets 'Harmful if eaten' names no animal and was not used.

chill_damage_f 40 comes from NC State's Description: 'It is hardy in frost free Zones 10-11, but will not tolerate temperatures below 40°F.', a cold-intolerance threshold recorded as the damage onset. The same page's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field lists 9a, 9b, 10a, 10b, 11a, 11b, which includes zones colder than 40°F, so the figure is in tension with NC State's own zone field. MoBot's Culture text gives only 'Hardy in frost free Zones 10-11.' and RHS rates it H1C; both are survival ratings, not onsets.

mature_height_in 120-240 and mature_spread_in 12-24 are NC State's Dimensions block (10-20 ft, 1-2 ft); this is a twining climber, so height is length on a support. RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres (157-315 in) and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in), which differ.
soil_ph left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) bands and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State prose says the plant will tolerate some shade, a conditional aside, so only full_sun is recorded; RHS also gives Full sun.

water_regime null: NC State's 'consistently moist, organically rich, well-draining soil' and MoBot's 'evenly moist, rich, well-draining soil' describe the soil, not a watering cadence. RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' and MoBot's structured Water: Medium are mid-scale ratings that do not support keep_moist. No admissible source gives a watering statement or schedule.

soil_base garden_bed: the sources describe outdoor garden soil (NC State 'organically rich, well-draining soil'; RHS planting locations include flower borders and beds), though NC State also lists Container and Patio locations and MoBot says it can be grown in a large container; no potting medium is specified. is_houseplant false: NC State's 'Keep the plant as a indoor plant or plant outdoors once the threat of frost has completely past.' is an option during the frost period, not a houseplant recommendation (the audit proposed null; this catalog lands landscape plants as false). No source gives a watering interval, humidity, light foot-candles, day/night temperatures or fertilizer.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's '6 or more hours' is its light-category legend text, not species prose.

records.name_note: The lead name is RHS's: its dedicated Nicotiana sylvestris page renders 'woodland tobacco plant' as the common name beneath the H1 (page title 'Nicotiana sylvestris | woodland tobacco plant') and lists flowering tobacco only under 'Other common names'. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for the same taxon is alphabetized -- Flowering Tobacco, South American Tobacco Plant, Tobacco Plant, White Shooting Stars, White Tobacco, Woodland Tobacco Plant -- and its description prose opens 'White shooting stars, or flowering tobacco plant'. Neither page uses the exact string 'Woodland Tobacco'; both use 'Woodland Tobacco Plant'. Flowering Tobacco is not used as the lead name because it is already the landed name of Nicotiana alata.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Nicotiana sylvestris page): the page states "This plant has high severity poison characteristics." and, in its human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans" block, Poison Severity: High; Poison Symptoms: "If ingested: abdominal pain, hypertension, tachycardia, tremors, progressing to hypotension, bradycardia, dyspnea, and respiratory failure."; Poison Toxic Principle: Nicotinic and nicotine-like alkaloids; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The severity rating comes from that human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block; the pet tags are separate. NC State's description text states "If ingested, toxic to humans, cats, dogs, and horses." Its Problems field lists: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. Its tag line includes #problem for cats #problem for dogs #problem for horses #poisonous if ingested #problem for children. Plant Type: Annual, Herbaceous Perennial. Handling warning (NC State): "Contact dermatitis: Avoid skin contact. Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling this plant. Glandular hairs on the leaves are sticky and may cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals." RHS: "Harmful if eaten; avoid skin contact. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and "Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten; avoid skin contact. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". The sources differ in breadth, not direction: RHS's pet line names dogs only ("Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten; avoid skin contact."), while NC State names humans, cats, dogs, and horses and also lists Problem for Children.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org could not be read (connect error and certificate verification failure), so it was not used; no other admissible domain was consulted beyond NC State and RHS. Nothing was added or repaired in the shared quote cache.

No admissible page I read says the exact string 'Woodland Tobacco'; both NC State and RHS say 'Woodland Tobacco Plant'. The common-name collision with Nicotiana alata (Flowering Tobacco) was not cross-cited to that species' page.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Plant Type (Annual, Herbaceous Perennial) and Landscape Location (Naturalized Area, Patio, Small Space, Walkways) fields and RHS's Flower borders and beds place it outdoors; no source read addresses indoor culture.
Soil pH left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together (open-ended bands) and RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no floor or ceiling is set.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific prose gives an hour figure; NC State's 2-6 hour and 6+ hour figures sit in its generic light-category legend.

water_regime keep_moist rests on RHS's structured Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' alone; NC State's 'consistently moist, well-drained soil' is a soil adjective and is not used for it. Neither source gives a watering instruction, so the dry-down and interval fields are null. The same RHS Moisture value was ruled a mid-scale rating that does not support keep_moist for Ipomoea lobata in this batch; the audit let this value stand, so it is kept, but it is a thin basis.

Size: NC State's dimensions (3-5 ft tall, 1 ft 2 in - 2 ft wide) are used as the anchor. RHS's Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) agrees with NC State's height; only its Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) is narrower than NC State's 14-24 in.
Hardiness: NC State says winter-hardy in zones 10-11 and plantable as an annual in NC; RHS lists a hardiness rating of H2. Neither is a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.
Temperature, humidity, indoor light, fertilizer and watering-interval fields are null: no admissible page I read supports them.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade; RHS Position lists Full sun, Partial shade; both agree. NC State also says it will appreciate some partial shade in the south's hot afternoon sun.
is_edible false is based on NC State's 'poisonous if ingested' tag and statement of toxicity if ingested, and RHS's 'Harmful if eaten'; no source describes any food use.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for Fragaria virginiana leads with Scarlett Strawberry (NC State's spelling): its page-title parenthetical reads "(Scarlett Strawberry, Wild Strawberry)", its alphabetized Common Name(s) list gives Scarlett Strawberry first and Wild Strawberry second, and its description opens "Scarlett Strawberry, also called Wild Strawberry". Scarlett Strawberry is therefore the common_name and Wild Strawberry is the alternate name. NC State's "is often confused with" module for this page names Potentilla indica. Only NC State had a usable page; no other admissible source was reachable for this taxon. Distinct from the garden Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page carries no Poison block. Its tag list reads "#specialized bees #nectar plant #edible garden #pollinator plant #NC native #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #bee friendly #wildlife friendly #beneficial insects #th-taste #th-wildlife", which includes "non-toxic for cats" and "non-toxic for dogs". Only NC State was found, so there is no second source and no disagreement to report. Edibility is the fruit: NC State's description calls the plant "a provider of edible fruit", its Fruit Value To Gardener field reads Edible, and its Edibility field says "Wild strawberries have a sweet tart flavor."; it gives no preparation instructions or part-specific restrictions.
unknowns: Only NC State Extension (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) was usable. The RHS URL guess returned 404, MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org and the www site) was blocked by the sandbox proxy, and Clemson HGIC returned 403, so no second admissible source was read. Every non-null field rests on NC State alone.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Plant Type (Native Plant, Wildflower) and zone range 5a-9b place it outdoors; its Container and Hanging Baskets Landscape Locations are outdoor use, and no admissible source addresses indoor culture.
toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' tags only. NC State has no Poison block for this page, and no second source was read.

is_edible=true: NC State describes the genus as 'producing edible fruit', lists Fruit Value To Gardener as Edible, and its Edibility field says 'Wild strawberries have a sweet tart flavor.' No preparation instructions, part restrictions or hazards are stated. The garden strawberry's (Fragaria x ananassa) yield and care claims were deliberately not carried over.

water_regime left null: 'moist to dry, well-drained soils' is a soil description and 'Drought' under Resistance To Challenges is a tolerance trait, so neither is a watering statement. NC State states no watering instruction.
soil_drainage=moderate from NC State's Soil Drainage tags 'Good Drainage', 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Dry'. Those tags span both the dry and the moist side, so they do not support fast.

soil_base=garden_bed rests on NC State's 'fertile, moist to dry, well-drained soils' and its erosion-control use on slopes. The culture is not exclusively in-ground: NC State also says "Use this plant in containers, on slopes, naturalized areas and native pollinator gardens.", but gives no potting-mix advice.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light tags are 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and the description says 'full sun to part shade'. Partial Shade is recorded as part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because those hour figures come from the site-wide tag legend, not species prose.

Soil pH, temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and chill-damage onset: not stated by NC State for this species, so left null. The description says only that it 'does not do well in summer heat and humidity', which is not a numeric figure. NC State's USDA zones 5a-9b are a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.
Mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block: Height 0 ft. 4 in. to 0 ft. 9 in. (4 to 9 in.) and Width 1 ft. 0 in. to 2 ft. 0 in. (12 to 24 in.).

NC State's Wildlife Value field names the specialized bee Andrena (Micrandrena) melanochroa for the genus Fragaria. It is not used as a species-level claim. attracts_pollinators rests on the Attracts field value 'Pollinators'.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's page title is 'Cornus mas | cornelian cherry', which leads with the binomial; cornelian cherry is RHS's headline common name, rendered beneath the H1, and RHS lists cornel, edible dogwood and sorbet under Other common names. NC State's page-title parenthetical, in alphabetical order, begins with Cornelia-Cherry and also lists Cornelia-Cherry Dogwood, Cornelian Cherry, Cornelian Cherry Dogwood and European Cornel; its rendered Common Name(s) list is in the same order. Cornelian Cherry was chosen because it is RHS's lead common name and it appears in NC State's list. NC State lists the previous names Cornus erythrocarpa, Cornus flava, Cornus mascula and Cornus vernalis. NC State's 'often confused with' module names Cornus officinalis, which is kept distinct from this record.
records.toxicity_detail: Neither the NC State nor the RHS page for Cornus mas states any toxicity to cats, dogs or people, and neither carries a Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, so toxic_to_pets is left null. Edibility, per NC State's Edibility field: 'Fruits are edible and may be used to make a tart jelly.' NC State's Fruit Description adds a ripeness condition: the fruits 'may be eaten when the fruit turns dark red.' No other plant part is addressed for eating.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is null: neither consulted source (NC State, RHS) states toxicity to cats or dogs. NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags (its only Problems tag is Weedy), and RHS's page has no toxicity statement.
is_houseplant false: neither page frames the plant as a houseplant; NC State lists it as an outdoor landscape shrub or tree (Plant Type Edible, Perennial, Shrub, Tree; zones 4a-8b).

Edibility is conditional: NC State says the fruits are edible and may be used to make a tart jelly, and may be eaten when the fruit turns dark red. Nothing on the NC State or RHS pages addresses eating other parts.
The MoBot, Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, Maryland and Georgia sources were not consulted for this record; only the NC State and RHS pages for this exact taxon were used.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, and RHS's Position lists Full sun and Partial shade, so full_sun and part_shade are recorded. NC State's Description prose says the plant 'prefers full to partial shade', which conflicts with its own structured Light field; full_shade is left out because neither structured field lists it.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figures are the generic range in NC State's site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no floor or ceiling can be set.
water_regime and the other watering fields are null: neither page states a watering recommendation. NC State's Moist drainage tag and RHS's Moisture field describe soil, not watering.

soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's bare Good Drainage plus Moist pair, RHS's 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' and NC State's 'moist, well-drained rich soils' prose all point to the middle of the scale.

Mature size: NC State's own page gives Height 15 ft. 0 in. - 25 ft. 0 in. (180-300 in) and Width 15 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in. (180-240 in), used as the anchor. RHS gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) with 10-20 years to maturity, a smaller UK-calibrated range that is not used.

No admissible source consulted gives temperature, humidity, light-intensity, fertilizing or chill-damage figures for this species; those fields are null. RHS's H6 hardiness rating is a survival rating, not a damage-onset temperature.

records.name_note: Led with Ramps because both dedicated admissible pages use it first: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for Allium tricoccum reads Ramps, Ramson, Spring Onion, Wild Leek (alphabetical, Ramps first; the page's H1 is the binomial alone), and Penn State titles its page Ramps (Allium tricoccum). records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source scopes any toxicity to cats or dogs, and NC State's page carries no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags and no Poison block with poison parts, symptoms or severity. NC State's Plant Type field lists exactly five values: Cool Season Vegetable, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Poisonous. The page does not say which part is poisonous, to whom, or why, and it carries no handling warning; read alongside its Edibility text, the Poisonous tag is unexplained, so edibility is conditional on correct identification; separately, NC State asks wild harvesters to leave the bulbs and one leaf in the ground to promote sustainability. NC State Edibility field: "Leaves, stems and bulbs have garlic onion flavor high in vitamin C. If harvesting in the wild, leave the bulbs and one leaf in the ground to promote sustainablity." NC State warns of poisonous look-alikes and Penn State calls them deadly poisonous: NC State says ramps have a distinct strong garlic/onion fragrance distinguishing it from the poisonous look-a-likes Lily of the valley or false hellebores; Penn State says lily-of-the-valley and false hellebore are deadly poisonous, can be found in the same habitat, and that ramps should always produce a notable onion and garlic smell when crushed or bruised. NC State's 'is often confused with' panel lists Allium tuberosum, Convallaria majalis and Veratrum viride. Neither page gives preparation times or doses.
